scenes.narration: You have fifty switches. You need to add one new V L A N. Do you really want to type it fifty times? V T P does it once.

scenes.heading: The library catalogue
scenes.narration: Imagine a library with many branches. One head librarian keeps the master catalogue, which is the V L A N database. When a new book arrives, the head librarian updates the catalogue and sends fresh index cards to every branch. That's a V T P advertisement. Branches can be servers, who can change the catalogue, clients, who only copy it, or transparent, who keep their own and just pass cards along. Every update has a revision number, and the higher number always wins.

scenes.heading: The three modes
scenes.narration: Here's how the modes behave. Servers create and delete V L A Ns, and share them. Clients can't create anything, they only learn. Transparent switches keep their own list, ignore the neighbours' updates, but still pass the messages on.

scenes.heading: Common mix-ups
scenes.narration: Three warnings. A client can't create V L A Ns locally. A transparent switch does forward updates, it just doesn't use them. And the revision number lives in a file called vlan dot dat, so reloading the switch does not reset it. That's how a lab switch with a high number can wipe out a whole network.

items.right: It's stored in vlan.dat; it survives a reload

scenes.heading: Remember this
scenes.narration: So, to recap. V T P copies the V L A N list from one server to every switch. Remember the three modes: server, client and transparent. And always reset the revision number before adding a switch. Ready to practise? Try the Courseiva VTP lab.
